full_judgment:
ABM Khairul Haque J: This death reference under section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure has been made by the Additional Sessions Judge, First Court, Barisal, for confirmation of sentence of death imposed upon the condemned prisoner Golam Mostafa and Shah Alam Kazi under section 302 of the Penal Code, by his judgment and order dated 29-9-1997, in Sessions Case No. 88 of 1996. By the said judgment he also found the appellants in Criminal Appeal No. 1868 of 1997, Criminal Appeal No. 2058 of 1997, Criminal Appeal No. 2018 of 1997, Criminal Appeal No. 2055 of 1997, Criminal Appeal No. 2300 of 1997 and Jail Appeal No. 1982 of 1997 guilty under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life and also to pay a fine of Taka 5,000 each with default order. Both the death reference and the appeals have been heard together and are disposed of by this judgment. 

 7. Mr Abdul Malek, the learned Senior Advocate, appears on behalf of the appellants in Criminal Appeal No. 1868 of 1997, Criminal Appeal No. 2055 of 1997, Criminal Appeal No. 2058 of 1997 and also in Jail Appeal No. 1982 of 1997 and Syed Ziaul Karim, the learned Advocate, appears on behalf of the appellants in Criminal Appeal No. 2018 of 1997 and Criminal Appeal No. 2300 of 1997. Mr Shamsuddin Ahmed Chowdhury, learned Deputy Attorney-General, appears with Syed Haider Ali, learned Assistant Attorney-General, on behalf of the State in the death reference as well as in all the criminal appeals and also in the jail appeal. 

 10. Mr A Malek, the learned Senior Counsel, appearing on behalf of both the condemned prisoners and other appellants in Criminal Appeal No. 1868 of 1997, Criminal Appeal No. 2055 of 1997 and Criminal Appeal No. 2058 of 1997, raised various points assailing the judgment and order passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge. He firstly, contends that in the instant case there was no first information report because police after hearing the gunshots at 8-45 AM recorded a general diary entry at 8-45 AM and, as such, if there was at all a first information report , the general diary should be treated as the first information report and not the one lodged by PW 1, since the said general diary was recorded earlier in point of time, and submits that any other information received by the police station subsequent to the said general diary entry, cannot be treated as a first information report as the very nomenclature suggests an information which was recorded earlier in point of time by the police, and in the instant case the general diary is the earliest record of the incident. The Deputy Attorney-General however, in reply, submits that general diary entry, in the facts and circumstances of this case, cannot be treated as a first information report because the said general diary entry recorded at 8-45 AM lacks in particulars of any offence of any kind and that there was no names, address, particulars of any kind of either of the informant or of the assailant or of any witness. Rather, he submits, the first information report lodged by PW 1 at 10-15 AM, records for the first time, information with regard to the offence committed which was signed by herself and recorded the detailed information not only of the allegations of murder but also the names and addresses of the assailants and the persons who saw the occurrence, as such, Exhibit 1 lodged by PW 1 was the first information report, as envisaged under section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In reply, Mr Malek submits that in similar circumstances in the case of Paran Chandra Baroi vs State 1982 BCR, 292 the Police on receipt of an information at about 12-30 PM through rumours that a person has been killed and his dead body was lying at Khair Math, recorded a general diary entry to that effect and rushed to the place of occurrence. There the concerned police officer after holding the inquest on the dead body at 14-00 hours sent it to the hospital for post mortem examination. In the meantime, the informant on receipt of the news, lodged a first information report at 19-00 hours but the said first information report, lodged by the father of the deceased, after commencement of the investigation, was held to be a statement before the police and the High Court Division, in those facts, held that there was no first information report in that case and ultimately, the convict-appellant was acquitted. On appeal, the Appellate Division although did not consider the question of first information report, upheld the order of acquittal passed by the High Court Division. This decision of the Appellate Division was reported in 1986 BCR (AD) 225. Relying on those decisions, Mr Malek submits that here in this case, since the police after recording the general diary, went to the place of occurrence, started inquest on the dead body and thereby started the investigation before lodging of the alleged first information report , there was no first information report in the eye of law, save and except the general diary entry recorded by the police at 8-45 AM. On the other hand, the learned Deputy Attorney-General refers to the case of Punhal Shah vs State 1984 PLD (SC) 62 and submits that in the instant case the first information report (Exhibit 1) was lodged immediately after commission of a cognizable offence leaving no scope for consultation and fabrication, cannot but be treated as the first information report . 

 11. In the Code of Criminal Procedure, no where is defined a general diary entry. It is available in section 44 of the Police Act (V of 1861) and the Regulations made thereunder. The police officers are obliged to record all information and steps taken by them in course of their duties in a diary known as General Diary as envisaged in section 44 of the Police Act and the Police Regulation, 1943. 

 14. He further submits that the first information report was lodged after completion of the inquest, as such, was hit by section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and cannot be used as an evidence or even as a first information report or for any other purpose by the prosecution. He submits, from the evidence, it is apparent that police reached the place of occurrence at 9-00 AM and at about 9-30 AM they started inquest of the dead body but the first information report was lodged with the police station at 10-15 AM, the said information cannot be treated as a first information report but may at best be a statement under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In reply, the learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that in this particular case the informant rushed to the police station immediately after the occurrence but no first information report was recorded and that upon going back to the place of occurrence, she wanted to state the incident but the police officer asked her to lodge the first information report in writing at the police station. The learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that there was no lathes on the part of the informant to lodge the first information report which under the circumstances, was properly done and there was no reason not to treat the said written information as the first information report. In this connection he refers to the decisions reported in 26 CrLJ 1213 and 38 DLR 289 and submits that in spite of the earlier starting of the inquest, the information (Exhibit 1) lodged by PW 1 was the actual first information report within the meaning of section 154 CrPC. 

 16. In the case of Touhid Alam vs State, 38 DLR 289, one Khalilur Rahman, a relation of the victim, informed the police about the missing of the victim and her husband also lodged a GD with the Police. The Police, on the basis of these information, went to the place of occurrence, recovered the dead body of the victim and after obtaining the post mortem report, lodged the first information report. The question arose in the said case, as to which information was the actual first information report. Latifur Rahman, J (as his Lordship then was) held: 

 19. In this connection it should also be remembered that although the first information report is not substantive evidence but it has its own importance as the first recorded version of the offence. In this connection, reference may be made to the case of the State vs Basirullah, 16 DLR 189. In the said case, Murshed, J (as his Lordship then was) observed as follows: 

 28. In the case of Priya Bala Das vs Ata, 22 DLR 582, the learned Additional Sessions Judge, disbelieved the evidence of prosecution witnesses by referring to the statements recorded by the investigating Officer under section 161 CrPC and acquitted the accused persons from the charge under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code but the High Court set aside the said order of acquittal and directed retrial.  48. In the result, this reference is rejected with the commutation of the sentence. The appeal No. 2018 of 1997 so far appellant Jamal, son of Saijuddin alias Noaka Mollah and Montu, son of Nur Mohammad Howlader are concerned is allowed and the Appeal No. 2058 of 1997 so far Atahar Ali Howlader, son of late Hatem Ali Howlader is concerned is allowed. The Appeal No. 1868 of 1997 of Shah Alam Kazi, son of late A Wahid Kazi, the Criminal Appeal No. 2018 of 1997 so far as the appellant Sharif Mofizur Rahman alias Nantu, son of A Majid, the Criminal Appeal No. 2055 of 1997 in respect of Jasimuddin (Babul), son of Afsaruddin and Bazlu Howlader, son of late Gafur Ali and the Criminal Appeal No. 2058 of 1997 in respect of Paritosh Dhupi, son of Nemai Dhupi are dismissed. The Criminal Appeal No. 2300 of 1997 of Sekander, son of Shafizuddin, is also dismissed. The Jail Appeal No. 1982 of 1997 filed by Golam Mostafa and Shah Alam Kazi are also dismissed with commutation of sentence to imprisonment for life. The appellants Jashimuddin alias Babul, son of Afsaruddin, Bazlu Howlader, son of late Gafur Ali, Sharif Mofizur Rahman alias Nantu, son of A Majid, Jamal, son of Sejuddin alias Noaka Mollah, Montu, son of Nur Mohammad Howlader are directed to surrender to their bail bonds immediately to serve out their respective sentences.
